Perhaps there may be something even of a more hidden mystery in the words of the Lord when he says: "their sons, who are here with me." Where "here," or how "with me"? Let him who has ears to hear, hear. We, meanwhile, say that our fathers were that former people, but we are their sons. They, therefore, because they sinned, were rejected and fell; but we, their sons, have risen up and been raised erect in their place, we who knew not good or evil. For we are of the nations, we who…

This fifth and likewise final vision of Balaam is now to be examined by us, concerning which, just as in the others, let us beseech the Lord that at the end He may not forsake us, so that we may be able to grasp the meaning of this vision too not far from the truth. Its beginning, then, is in these words: "And when Balaam saw Amalek," it says, "taking up his parable, he said: The beginning of the nations is Amalek, and their seed shall perish." It seems necessary to me to search out in the divine Scriptures in what places or at what time the name of Amalek is written, and from what stock that nation descends. For what is sought will be more easily recognized if it is brought forward from the several places that are written about the same matter. Therefore in the reading of Genesis, where five kings assembled to make war upon the four kings who were reigning in Sodom, after some space it…

This Amalek, therefore, seeing him, Balaam the son of Beor, a man truly seeing and hearing the words of God, who knows the knowledge of the Most High and sees the visions of God, having taken up his parable as is written in the earlier visions also, says: "The beginning of the nations is Amalek, and their seed shall perish." As for what he says: "The beginning of the nations is Amalek," it is certain that it can in no way be referred to that Amalek who then existed in the flesh, for neither was he first in the antiquity of origin, but it is better referred to the invisible Amalek, who from turning the peoples aside from God and making Gentiles out of the worshipers of God is named Amalek. And therefore he is rightly called the beginning of the nations, as being a certain such adverse power which first gave the beginning for men to become Gentiles, by changing the glory of the…

The second festival, then, after the festival of the unceasing sacrifice, is set the sacrifice of the sabbath, and every holy and just man ought to keep also the festival of the sabbath. But what is the festival of the sabbath except that of which the Apostle says: "There remaineth therefore a sabbath-keeping," that is, an observance of the sabbath, "for the people of God"? Leaving aside, therefore, the Jewish observances of the sabbath, let us see of what sort the Christian's observance of the sabbath ought to be. On the sabbath day one ought to do no work out of all the works of the world. If, therefore, you cease from all secular works and do nothing worldly, but have leisure for spiritual works, come together to the church, lend an ear to the divine readings and expositions, think upon heavenly things, take thought for the hope to come, keep the judgment that is to come before your…

There follows after these things a station which is called Gai, which is interpreted "chaos." For through these journeyings one draws near to the bosom of Abraham, who says to those who are in torments that "between you and us a great chaos has been established," so that he too may rest in his bosom like that blessed Lazarus.

We say therefore with confidence that according to the Scriptures God does not know all. God does not know sin, and God does not know sinners; those estranged from himself he does not recognize. Hear the Scripture saying: "The Lord has known those who are his, and: let everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord depart from iniquity." The Lord knows his own, but the wicked and the impious he does not know. Hear the Savior saying: "Depart from me all you workers of iniquity, I have not known you." And again Paul says: "If anyone among you is a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that the things I write are the Lord's. But he who is ignorant, is ignored." But we say these things not perceiving anything blasphemous about God, as you do, nor ascribing ignorance to him, but we understand it thus, that those whose deed is unworthy of God are also deemed unworthy of the knowledge of God.…

Thence a station is held at Makheloth, which is interpreted "from the beginning." For he who tends toward perfection contemplates the beginning of things, nay rather refers all things to him who was in the beginning, and never departs from that beginning.

The reading recited today contains, first, a piece of history about the fornication of an Israelite man and a Midianite woman, and second, about the visitation of the people, in which it is commanded that they again be numbered by the precept of the Lord, the former number having, of course, been made void on account of the sins which those had committed who had earlier been enrolled under the reckoning of the number. Therefore the number that had been written down is cancelled and rendered void because of sins, and offenses have such power that not even this profits a man — that he had been counted in the number in God's sight — once he has turned aside. But, as Scripture reports, even the limbs of those who withdrew from God fell in the desert. There are, then, two histories that have been recited; but we, for the present, will speak of the first, which describes the fornication of…

"But Israel sojourned at Shittim." In the interpretation of Hebrew names we find that Shittim, in our language, is said to mean "answer" or "refutation." Israel, then, sojourned at "answer" or "refutation." It did not sojourn well. See, finally, what it ran into, placed in this station. It committed fornication with the Midianite women and was refuted by God, because not only did it commit fornication, but it was also consecrated to the idols of the nations and ate of those things which had been sacrificed to idols — things which are altogether execrable in God's sight. For what agreement has the temple of God with idols? Indeed I have also greatly wondered at those things which the Apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying: "But if anyone sees you, who have knowledge, reclining in an idol's temple, will not his conscience, since it is weak, be built up to eat things sacrificed to…

"And Edom shall be an inheritance, and Esau his enemy shall be an inheritance." Edom is the same as Esau. He according to history indeed is the enemy of Israel, but at the coming, he says, of Christ, he too shall be his inheritance, that is, he shall be received unto the faith and shall not be excluded from the inheritance of Christ. But if we consider it spiritually, Edom is understood as the flesh, which is opposed to the spirit and is its enemy. At the coming, then, of Christ, when the flesh shall have been subjected to the spirit, through the hope of resurrection it too shall come to the inheritance. For not the soul alone, but also the flesh, which once had been an enemy, through the obedience of the spirit shall become a sharer of the inheritance to come. "And Israel did it in power." This is what he says: that then Edom or Esau, that is, the nature of the flesh, shall be called…

But after a few words it is reported concerning that very city: "For this reason," he says, "the riddlers shall say: come into Heshbon, that the city of Sihon may be built and constructed; for fire went forth from Heshbon and a flame from the city of Sihon, and it devoured as far as Moab." Sihon, as we said, was the king, whose city was Heshbon. Thus, then, the order of the words is to be understood, that these riddlers say: come, that Heshbon, which was the city of Sihon, may be built and constructed. But let us now inquire who these riddlers are. A riddle is a figured saying; riddlers therefore are those who speak figuratively. And who else is there who has spoken in figures except the law and the prophets? For hear how David says: "I will open my mouth in parables, I will utter propositions from the beginning." But Isaiah too, that the things he wrote are riddles, declares in this…

After these things they come to Libnah. But Libnah is interpreted "praise of judgment." Most justly does praise follow after labors. Yet of what thing is it the praise? "Of judgment," he says. Worthy of praise, therefore, becomes the soul that judges rightly, discerns rightly — that is, which spiritually judges all things, and is itself judged by no one.
When you have passed through these, you will halt in Jotbathah. Jotbathah is interpreted "good things." To good things, therefore, one comes only after the trials of temptations.

"And the Egyptians," it says, "were burying their dead"; the dead were burying their dead, but the living were following the Lord their God. After this it is said that: "and upon their gods the Lord took vengeance." But in Exodus too it says thus: "and upon all the gods of the Egyptians the Lord shall take vengeance." Here, however, it says that the Lord took vengeance upon them. There are certain beings which are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, the Apostle says. But in the Psalms too it is said: "all the gods of the nations are demons." Therefore it is not the images, but the demons who preside over the images, that he calls gods, upon whom the Lord took vengeance. But I should like to inquire how God takes vengeance upon the demons, since assuredly the day of vengeance and of judgment has not yet come. But I think that this vengeance is wrought upon the demons when he who…

At this Balak, thinking that Balaam had been terrified by the multitude of the Israelite people and had therefore not dared to utter curses, believed that a change of place would profit him, and says to him: "Come yet with me to another place, from which you will not see them, but you will see some part of them, though you will not see them all, and curse them for me from there." Mad man, who would believe that the grace of Israel could be concealed by the interposition of a place, and who did not know that a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.

They set out therefore from Rithmah and come to Rimmon-perez. Rimmon-perez is interpreted "labors." And do not wonder if labors follow upon health. For the soul obtains health from God precisely for this, that it may take up labors with delight and not unwillingly; for it will be said to it: "You shall eat the labors of your fruits, blessed are you, and it shall be well with you."

With God, as we are given to understand, nothing is useless, nothing idle; but even those things which seem fit to be alienated and cast away by men are found to have some necessary function. This understanding is suggested to us by the present reading, which makes mention of the censers of Korah and of the rest who sinned along with him — that God commands that not even these be thrown away, but that from them beaten plates be made, and that the altar be encircled with them. Scripture therefore relates that, by the command of God, "Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest took," it says, "the bronze censers, which those who were burned up had offered, and they made of them plates, and set them upon the altar, for a memorial to the children of Israel, that no stranger who is not of the seed of Aaron should draw near to lay incense before the Lord, lest it should happen as with Korah and his…
After these things one comes to Haradah, which in our language sounds "made fit"; assuredly so that the soul too may say: "He has made us fit ministers of the new testament."

But in what follows also the reading which was recited contains this, that Moses took the Ethiopian woman as his wife, and that Miriam and Aaron disparaged Moses, because he had taken the Ethiopian woman, and they say: "Has God spoken to Moses alone? Has He not also spoken to us?" "And the Lord heard," it says. And after these things He orders them to go out to the tabernacle of the testimony, and there, a certain judgment having been held, Miriam is made leprous until a fixed time, and thus is called back into the camp. That we may explain this more concisely, we say that Miriam had the figure of the former people, and that Moses, that is, the law of the Lord, passed over to marriage with this Ethiopian woman, who was gathered from among the nations. Her, therefore, Moses, that is, the spiritual law, took as wife; and on account of this deed Miriam, who is now the synagogue, is…

Just as the Apostle says: "all these things happened to them as figures, but they were written for our admonition," I ask what admonition we may receive from that which has been read to us, namely that Aaron and Miriam spoke against Moses and on account of this were rebuked, and Miriam indeed was even made a leper. And so great was the concern of this rebuke that, while Miriam was completing the space of a week in leprosy, the people of God did not make their journey toward the land of promise, nor was the tabernacle of testimony moved. First of all, meanwhile, I am admonished, and usefully and necessarily admonished, from this deed, not to disparage my brother, not to speak evil of my neighbor, not to open my mouth to detract not only from the saints but even from any of my neighbors whatsoever, seeing how great was the indignation of God from this, how great a vengeance proceeded.…

After these things one now comes to Almon-diblathaim, which is interpreted "contempt of figs," that is, where earthly things are utterly despised and looked down upon. For unless those things which seem to delight on earth have been spurned and despised, we cannot pass over to the heavenly things.

After this: "Behold," it says, "a people shall rise up like a lion's cub, and shall exult like a lion." In these words he seems to me to describe the confidence of the people believing in Christ, and the freedom which it has in faith, and the exultation which it bears in hope. For it is compared to a lion's cub while it presses toward perfection, glad and swift; but it is likened to a lion when it now obtains the things that are perfect. For just as the lion and the lion's cub fear no animal, no beast, but all things are subjected to them, so also to the perfect Christian, who takes up his cross and follows Christ, who can say: "For to me the world is crucified, and I to the world," all things are subjected, all things are trodden underfoot. For he despises and scorns all things that are in this world, and imitates him who is called the lion of the tribe of Judah and the lion's cub,…

"It shall not sleep until it devours the prey, and drinks the blood of the slain." In these words, who will be so contentious a champion of the historical narrative — nay rather, who will be found so brutish — as not to flee, shuddering at the sound of the letter, by very necessity to the sweetness of allegory? For how will this people, so praiseworthy, so magnificent, of which the discourse recounts such great praises, come to this, that it should drink the blood of the slain — when the eating of blood is forbidden by God with such strong precepts, so that even we who have been called from the gentiles are necessarily commanded to abstain, just as from the things sacrificed to idols, so also from blood? Let them tell us, then, who is this people that has the practice of drinking blood. These were the things which, hearing them in the Gospel also, those who followed the Lord from among…

After these things one arrives at Ezion-geber, which is interpreted "the counsels of a man." If anyone has ceased to be a child in his senses, he arrives at the counsels of a man, just as also that one who said: "But when I became a man, I put away the things that were of a little one." Great, therefore, are the counsels of a man, just as that one too says: "Deep water is counsel in the heart of a man."

There were five daughters, whose names too are recorded in Scripture, born of a certain Israelite named Zelophehad, who died in the desert leaving behind no male offspring. These daughters of Zelophehad therefore approach Moses and demand a share of their father's inheritance, saying: let not the name of their father be blotted out from the midst of his people, because no son was born to him. On this matter Moses refers the question to God. But the mercy of Almighty God does not spurn or despise a consultation offered by young women, and not only deigns to give an answer, but so approves and embraces their words that from them he establishes eternal laws for men, to be observed for all ages. For the Lord says, speaking to Moses: the daughters of Zelophehad have spoken rightly; you shall give them a possession in the midst of their father's brothers, and you shall give the inheritance of…

"They set out," it says, "from the bitter waters and came to Elim." Elim is where there are twelve springs of water, and seventy-two palm trees. You see, after the bitter waters, after the harshness of trials, how pleasant are the places that receive you. You would not have come to the palms unless you had endured the bitter waters of trials, nor would you have come to the sweetness of the springs unless you had first overcome the things that were grievous and harsh; not that the end of the journey and the perfection of all things is already in these things, but that God, the steward of souls, interposes in the very course of the journey certain refreshments amid the labors, by which the soul, revived and restored, may return more ready to the remaining labors. Elim, however, is interpreted "rams." Rams are the leaders of flocks. Who then are the leaders of the flock of Christ, if not…

But that you may know that the king thought something of this sort, understand it from the words of Scripture, which I learned expounded by a certain teacher who had come to believe from among the Hebrews. It is written thus: "And Moab said to the elders of Midian: now this assembly will lick up all who are round about us, as the calf licks up the grass of the field." That teacher, then, who had come to believe from among the Hebrews, would say: why, he says, did he use such an example, saying: as the calf licks up the grass of the field? For this reason, without doubt, because the calf breaks off the grass from the field with its mouth and with its tongue, as with a sickle, cuts whatever it finds; so also this people, like a calf, fights with mouth and lips and has its arms in words and prayers. Knowing this, therefore, the king sends to Balaam, that he too may deliver words contrary…

And Moses said to Aaron: "Take the censer, and put fire upon it from the altar, and cast incense upon it, and carry it swiftly into the camp, and make entreaty for them; for wrath has gone forth from the presence of the Lord, and it has already begun to lay waste the people." But since we have come to these passages, I wish to admonish the disciples of Christ concerning the goodness of God, lest perhaps any of you be troubled by the heretics, if ever a controversy should arise, when they say that the God of the law is not good, but just, and that the law of Moses does not contain goodness, but justice. Let those, therefore, who alike accuse both God and the law, see how Moses himself and Aaron did earlier that which the gospel afterward taught. Behold, Moses loves his enemies and prays for his persecutors, which indeed Christ teaches to be done in the gospels. For hear how, falling on…

These are the numbers we are reading, and in the earlier reading we were shut out by time from saying anything about the second numbering; but it is fitting now to render what was omitted or left out. Therefore by the Lord's command the people was first numbered, but since those who had first been enrolled fell on account of their persistence in sins, a second people now, which succeeded into the place of the fallen by a revived generation, is called to the numbering, and what had not been said of those former ones is said of these. For after the number was gathered by tribes and peoples and houses and families, the Lord says to Moses: "To these the land shall be distributed by lot according to the number of names. To the more numerous more shall be given by lot, and to the small you shall give a small inheritance." If it had been said of the former ones that "to these the land shall be…

He says therefore: "According to the number of names, to the more numerous more shall be given by lot, and to the small you shall give a small inheritance; to each, as he has been counted, his inheritance shall be given." This is what the history teaches, that if any tribe is held to be more numerous among the peoples, it should obtain by lot larger tracts of land; but if any is reckoned with a smaller number of men, it should be content with a smaller possession. But since we say that the division of this land and the earthly inheritance holds the appearance and shows the image and form of those future goods, of that heavenly inheritance which is hoped for by the faithful and the saints, I inquire, in that inheritance which is to be hoped for, who are the many and who are the few, and I find that there the few are held more blessed than the many. For those who travel their journey by…

If, then, as we have said, the law has a shadow of the good things to come, and those who serve in the law serve a copy and shadow of heavenly things, and now the contemplation of realities is had through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face—I believe also that, whereas we are now said to have our conversation in the heavens through an appearance and in an enigma, then, however, those who shall deserve it will have their conversation in the heavens face to face. If, then, by the logical consequence of things and the faith of the promises, we must be transferred from the earth to heaven, I think that in those very heavenly places our Lord Jesus establishes each one, not apart from the lot of his merits, in this or that part and dwelling of heaven. But just as there is much difference on earth—for example, to dwell in fertile and abundant places, rich in all good things, where…

After this: "There shall be no labor," he says, "in Jacob, nor shall sorrow be seen in Israel." Openly in these words he announces the state of the life to come; for who is there who passes through this life without labor and sorrow? Not even if one be a Peter or a Paul. How is he not in labor and sorrow, when he is thrice beaten with rods, once stoned, thrice shipwrecked, is in the deep of the sea a day and a night, and endures countless other things which he writes about his labors and sorrows? But this will be fulfilled there, where it is said: "Sorrow and sadness and groaning have fled away." Yet this refers not to all, but only to those who by their merits shall have been Jacob and Israel; as was also that poor Lazarus, who indeed passed the present life in labor and sorrow, but there it is said to the rich man: "Remember, son, that you received your good things in your life, and…

"The Lord his God is with him, the glories of princes are with him." For God never deserts his Israel. But let us see of what princes the glories are with this Israel. The glory of princes is power, principality, and kingdom. But since there are also certain princes who are to be driven from their principality, or perhaps have already been driven out, and into their place and principality are to be introduced those who are truly Israelites — all those glories which those princes had in the heavens, princes who did not keep their principality but forsook their eternal dwellings, this Israel and Jacob, who wrestled and prevailed, shall receive; and thus the glories of princes shall be with him.

Now from here a station is held at Moseroth, which is thought to signify "excluding." Excluding whom? Without doubt the malignant suggestions of the contrary spirit from one's thoughts. For thus also the Wisdom of God says: "If the spirit of one having power ascend upon you, leave not your place." The place therefore must be held, and the adversary must be excluded, lest he find a place in our heart, as the Apostle says: "Do not give place to the devil."

Yesterday we spoke of how Sihon, king of the Amorites, who is the lofty one and the barren tree, having engaged with Israel was defeated; concerning whom Scripture also says pointedly that he fell "by the slaughter of the sword" or, as we read elsewhere, "by the mouth of the sword." But if you wish to know more carefully by what sword this barren and lofty one, "like the cedar of Lebanon," fell, let us learn from the Apostle Paul, who says: "For the word of God is living and effective and more piercing than any sword," and again in another place: "and the sword," he says, "of the spirit, which is the word of God." By the slaughter of this sword, then, fell the spiritual Sihon, who is the devil. After these things it is added: "and the sons of Israel," he says, "had dominion over all his land." All this earthly region indeed is called the land of Sihon, but Christ and his Church have…

After these things one comes to Libnah, which is interpreted "whitening." I know that in other places whitening is set down blameworthily, as when it is said "whitewashed wall" and "whitewashed tombs." But here that whitening is meant, of which the prophet says: "You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow"; and again Isaiah: "If your sins be as scarlet, I will whiten them as snow, and make them white as wool"; and likewise in the psalm: "They shall be whitened with snow in Salmon"; and the hairs of the Ancient of days are said to be white, that is, white as wool. So therefore this whitening is to be understood as coming from the splendor of the true light and as descending from the brightness of heavenly visions.

After these things a station is made at Tahath, which is "confirmation" or "patience." For it is necessary that he who wishes to be of profit to others also should suffer many things and bear all things patiently, just as it was said of Paul: "For I will show him how great things he must suffer for my name."

But meanwhile the present reading contains certain distinctions among vows. For if it be a man who vows, he is said to be free in his vows and subject to no one. But if a woman vows, then, if indeed she be in her father's house, her vow hangs upon her father's judgment; and if he refuses it, she is released; but if he does not refuse it, both he and the daughter are held liable. But if, after the father has not refused, she does not fulfill the vow, the daughter's sin remains upon him. And in like manner it is decreed also concerning the husband, that, if a wife has vowed something in her husband's house and the husband on hearing it does not refuse, he is guilty of the vow equally with his wife; but if he refuses, then the wife is as free as the husband; but if he keeps silent, both, as we have said, are held guilty. These indeed are the things that are written; but we must pray to God…

After these things one comes to Hazeroth, which is interpreted "perfect courts" or "blessedness." Look more diligently, O my traveler, what is the order of the journeyings: after you have buried and handed over to death the concupiscences of the flesh, you will come to the spaciousness of the courts, you will come to blessedness. For blessed is the soul which is now pressed by no vices of the flesh.

For tell me, was it not God who commanded by Moses that no image or likeness of anything which was in heaven above or which was on the earth should be made, and yet who caused the brazen serpent to be made by Moses in the wilderness, and set it up for a sign by which those bitten by serpents were saved? Yet is He free from unrighteousness. For by this, as I previously remarked, He proclaimed the mystery, by which He declared that He would break the power of the serpent which occasioned the transgression of Adam, and [would bring] to them that believe on Him [who was foreshadowed] by this sign, i.e., Him who was to be crucified, salvation from the fangs of the serpent, which are wicked deeds, idolatries, and other unrighteous acts.

As far as that goes, we too have examples from this same past in favor of our own way of thinking, examples of a judgment on fornication which was not only not remiss but rather immediately executed. It is quite enough, I should think, that so great a number of the chosen people, twenty-four thousand, perished at one stroke after they had fornicated with the daughters of Midian. I prefer, however, for the glory of Christ, to derive ecclesiastical discipline from Christ.

The prophet Balaam, in Numbers, was sent forth by king Balak to curse Israel, with whom he was commencing war. But at the same moment he was filled with the spirit. Instead of the curse which he came to pronounce, he uttered the blessing which the spirit at that very hour inspired him with. This is he who had previously declared to the king's messengers, and then to the king himself, that he could only speak forth that which God should put into his mouth. The novel [heretical] doctrines of the new Christ are such as the Creator's servants initiated long before!

Later on, a sacred vine put forth a cluster of grapes that was prophetic. To those who had been led by the Educator to a place of rest after their wanderings it was a sign, for the great cluster of grapes is the Word crushed on our account. The Word desired that the "blood of the grape" be mixed with water as a symbol that his own blood is an integral element in salvation.

Hence is that which is said to the Cinite, by Balaam when prophesying, Strong indeed is thy dwelling place, but if thou hast placed thy nest in the rock. For Cinite is interpreted 'possessor.' And who are they who possess present things, except those who are skilled in the ability of worldly wisdom? And they truly build themselves therein a strong dwelling place, if becoming, by humility, as little children in their own sight, they are nourished in the sublimity of Christ; if they feel themselves to be weak, and give up the confidence of their mind, to be cherished by the lofty humility of the Redeemer Who is known to them; if they seek not after things below; if they pass over, with the flight of their heart, every thing which passes away. Let us behold the eagle building itself the nest of hope in high places. He says; Our conversation is in heaven. And again; Who hath raised us up…

quotes.quote: To leave the crowds and return to the tabernacle means to leave the tumult of external things behind and enter the hidden places of the mind. For the Lord is consulted there, and one hears, silently and within, what should be done outside and publicly. Good pastors do this every day. When they do not know how to decide about doubtful matters, they return to the hidden place of the mind as if to some tabernacle. They ponder the divine law, as if they were seeking advice from the Lord at the ark of the covenant. What they first hear silently within, they later make known when they act publicly. To fulfill their external offices without blame, they have recourse unceasingly to the secret places of the heart, and thus they hear the voice of God through his hidden inspiration, as they withdraw from carnal sensations in spiritual meditation. Every only child is a firstborn child; but not every firstborn is an only child. A firstborn child is not only one after whom other children are also born but also one before whom no other child is born. "All that opens the womb," says the Lord to Aaron, "of all flesh that are offered to the Lord, of men and beasts, shall belong to you; only the firstborn of men shall be redeemed with a price and the firstborn of beasts that are unclean." The Word of God defined what was meant by a "firstborn." "All," it says, "that opens the womb." Otherwise, if no child is a firstborn child but only one who subsequently has brothers, the firstborn are not due the priests until others are also born, lest perchance a child be an only child and not the firstborn child, in the event that no other child shall be born subsequently.

quotes.quote: BY WHAT REASONING DID THE CHALDEAN MAGI UNDERSTAND, FROM THE APPEARANCE OF A STAR, THAT CHRIST, THE KING OF THE JEWS, HAD BEEN BORN, SINCE A TEMPORAL KING IS USUALLY SIGNIFIED BY A STAR AS A SIGN (Matt. 2:1–2)? — These Chaldean Magi did not observe the course of the stars out of malevolence, but out of a curiosity about things. For, as can be understood, they were following the tradition of Balaam: who, when he had been summoned by Balak to curse the people of God, by divine prompting began to bless them. quotes.quote: IF THE WILL OF THE RIGHTEOUS MAN IS GOOD, WHY DID NOT ISAAC BLESS ESAU AS HE WISHED, BUT JACOB WHOM HE WOULD NOT BLESS? — The righteous man’s will is good, as far as his own conscience is concerned; but with respect to foreknowledge, it is free from opposing events.
